danish.title: Tredje bog (1805) — Kapitel 19
paragraphs: På Pratzen-højderne, hvor han var faldet med fanestangen i hånden, lå fyrst Andrej Bolkonskij og blødte voldsomt, mens han ubevidst udstødte en svag, ynkelig og barnlig klynken.

Hen mod aften holdt han op med at klynke og blev helt stille. Han vidste ikke, hvor længe hans bevidstløshed varede. Pludselig fornemmede han igen, at han levede og led af en brændende, sønderrivende smerte i hovedet.

»Hvor er den — den høje himmel, som jeg ikke kendte før i dag, men så i dag?« var hans første tanke. »Og denne lidelse kendte jeg heller ikke,« tænkte han. »Ja, jeg kendte ingenting, slet ingenting indtil nu. Men hvor er jeg?«

Han lyttede og hørte lyden af heste, der nærmede sig, og stemmer, der talte fransk. Han åbnede øjnene. Over ham var igen den samme høje himmel med skyer, der var steget op og nu svævede endnu højere, og imellem dem glimtede blå uendelighed. Han vendte ikke hovedet og så ikke dem, der, at dømme efter lyden af hove og stemmer, var redet hen til ham og standset.

Det var Napoleon ledsaget af to adjudanter. Bonaparte, der havde redet over slagmarken og givet sine endelige ordrer om at forstærke batterierne, der beskød Augesd-dæmningen, betragtede de dræbte og sårede, der var efterladt på marken.
»Smukke mænd!« bemærkede Napoleon, idet han betragtede en død russisk grenader, der lå på maven med ansigtet begravet i jorden og en allerede stivnet arm udslynget til siden, med en sortfarvet nakke.
»Ammunitionen til kanonerne i stilling er opbrugt, Deres Majestæt,« sagde en adjudant, der var kommet fra batterierne, som beskød Augesd.

»Lad noget hente fra reserven,« sagde Napoleon, og efter at have gået videre et par skridt standsede han foran fyrst Andrej, der lå på ryggen med fanestangen kastet ved siden af sig. (Fanen var allerede blevet taget af franskmændene som krigsbytte.)
»Det er en smuk død!« sagde Napoleon, idet han betragtede Bolkonskij.

Fyrst Andrej forstod, at det blev sagt om ham, og at det var Napoleon, der sagde det. Han hørte taleren blive tiltalt som Sire. Men han hørte ordene, som han ville have hørt en flues summen. De interesserede ham ikke blot ikke, han lagde ikke engang mærke til dem og glemte dem øjeblikkeligt. Hans hoved brændte, han følte, at han forblødte, og over sig så han den fjerne, høje og evige himmel. Han vidste, det var Napoleon — hans helt — men i det øjeblik forekom Napoleon ham et så lille, ubetydeligt væsen sammenlignet med det, der nu foregik mellem ham selv og den høje uendelige himmel med sine drivende skyer. I det øjeblik betød det intet for ham, hvem der stod over ham, eller hvad der blev sagt om ham; han var blot glad for, at der stod mennesker i nærheden, og ønskede kun, at de ville hjælpe ham og bringe ham tilbage til livet, som nu forekom ham så smukt, efter at han i dag havde lært at forstå det helt anderledes. Han samlede alle sine kræfter for at røre sig og frembringe en lyd. Han bevægede svagt sit ben og udstødte en svag, syg klynken, der vakte hans egen medlidenhed.
»Ah! Han lever,« sagde Napoleon. »Løft denne unge mand op og bring ham til forbindingsstationen.«
Efter at have sagt dette red Napoleon videre for at møde marskal Lannes, der kom ridende med hatten i hånden og smilende hilste kejseren for at lykønske ham med sejren.

Fyrst Andrej huskede intet mere: han mistede bevidstheden af den forfærdelige smerte, da han blev løftet op på båren, af rystelserne under transporten og af undersøgelsen af hans sår på forbindingsstationen. Han kom først til bevidsthed sent på dagen, da han sammen med andre sårede og tilfangetagne russiske officerer blev bragt til hospitalet. Under denne transport følte han sig en smule stærkere og var i stand til at se sig omkring og endda tale.

De første ord, han hørte, da han kom til bevidsthed, var en fransk konvojofficers, der hurtigt sagde: »Vi må gøre holdt her: kejseren vil passere her snart; det vil glæde ham at se disse herrer fanger.«
»Der er så mange fanger i dag — næsten hele den russiske hær — at han sikkert er træt af dem,« sagde en anden officer.
»Lige meget! Man siger, at denne her er kommandør for hele kejser Aleksandrs garde,« sagde den første og pegede på en russisk officer i hestegardernes hvide uniform.
Bolkonskij genkendte fyrst Repnin, som han havde mødt i det petersborgske selskabsliv. Ved siden af ham stod en dreng på nitten, også en såret officer fra hestegarden.
Bonaparte, der var kommet til i galop, standsede sin hest.
»Hvem er den øverste i rang?« spurgte han ved synet af fangerne.
De nævnte obersten, fyrst Repnin.
»De er kommandør for kejser Aleksandrs hestegardistregiment?« spurgte Napoleon.
»Jeg kommanderede en eskadron,« svarede Repnin.
»Deres regiment opfyldte sin pligt med ære,« sagde Napoleon.
»En stor feltherres ros er en soldats højeste belønning,« sagde Repnin.
»Jeg giver den med fornøjelse,« sagde Napoleon. »Og hvem er den unge mand ved Deres side?«
Fyrst Repnin nævnte løjtnant Sukhtelen.
Napoleon så på ham og smilede.
»Han er meget ung til at blande sig med os.«
»Ungdom er ingen hindring for mod,« mumlede Sukhtelen med svag stemme.
»Et glimrende svar!« sagde Napoleon. »Unge mand, De vil nå langt!«

Fyrst Andrej, som også var blevet ført frem for kejserens øjne for at fuldende opvisningen af fanger, kunne ikke undgå at tiltrække sig hans opmærksomhed. Napoleon huskede tilsyneladende at have set ham på slagmarken og brugte igen den betegnelse »unge mand«, som i hans erindring var knyttet til fyrst Andrej.
»Nå, og De, unge mand,« sagde han. »Hvordan har De det, mon brave?«

Selvom fyrst Andrej fem minutter forinden havde kunnet sige et par ord til de soldater, der bar ham, var han nu tavs med blikket stift rettet mod Napoleon... Så ubetydelige syntes ham i det øjeblik alle de interesser, der optog Napoleon, så ringe forekom hans helt selv med sin smålige forfængelighed og sejrsglæde sammenlignet med den ophøjede, retfærdige og milde himmel, han havde set og forstået, at han ikke kunne svare ham.

Alt syntes så meningsløst og ubetydeligt i sammenligning med den strenge og højtidelige tankerække, som svækkelsen fra blodtab, lidelsen og nærheden af døden vakte i ham. Idet han så Napoleon i øjnene, tænkte fyrst Andrej på storhedens ubetydelighed, livets uvæsentlighed, som ingen kunne forstå, og den endnu større uvæsentlighed af døden, hvis mening ingen levende kunne fatte eller forklare.

Kejseren vendte sig uden at vente på svar og sagde til en af officererne, idet han gik: »Sørg for disse herrer og bring dem til mit bivuak; lad min læge Larrey undersøge deres sår. Farvel, fyrst Repnin!« Og han satte sporerne i og galopperede bort.
Hans ansigt strålede af selvtilfredshed og glæde.

De soldater, der havde båret fyrst Andrej, havde bemærket og taget det lille guldikon, som fyrstinde Marja (hans søster) havde hængt om sin brors hals, men da de så kejserens velvilje mod fangerne, skyndte de sig at give det hellige billede tilbage.
Fyrst Andrej så ikke, hvordan og af hvem det blev sat på plads, men det lille ikon med sin tynde guldkæde dukkede pludselig op på hans bryst uden på uniformen.

»Det ville være godt,« tænkte fyrst Andrej, idet han betragtede det ikon, hans søster med så megen inderlighed og ærefrygt havde hængt om hans hals, »det ville være godt, hvis alting var så klart og enkelt, som det forekommer Marja. Hvor ville det være dejligt at vide, hvor man skal søge hjælp i dette liv, og hvad man kan vente sig hinsides graven! Hvor lykkelig og rolig ville jeg være, hvis jeg nu kunne sige: 'Herre, forbarm dig over mig!'... Men til hvem skulle jeg sige det? Enten til en kraft, der er udefinerbar og ubegribelig, som jeg ikke blot ikke kan henvende mig til, men som jeg end ikke kan udtrykke i ord — det Store Alt eller Intet,« sagde han til sig selv, »eller til den Gud, som Marja har syet ind i dette amulet! Der er intet sikkert, slet intet, undtagen alt dets ubetydelighed, som jeg forstår, og storheden af noget ufatteligt, men altafgørende.«

Bårene blev båret videre. Ved hvert stød følte han uudholdelig smerte; hans feber steg, og han blev delirisk. Visioner af hans far, hans kone, hans søster og hans kommende søn, og den ømhed, han havde følt natten før slaget, den ubetydelige lille Napoleons skikkelse, og over alt dette den høje himmel — det var hovedindholdet af hans feberdrømme.

Det stille hjemmeliv og den fredelige lykke på Lyse Bjerge (Bald Hills) stod ham for øje. Han nød allerede denne lykke, da den lille Napoleon pludselig dukkede op med sit usympatiske blik, der bar præg af kortsynet fryd over andres ulykke, og tvivl og kvaler havde fulgt, og kun himlen lovede fred. Hen mod morgenen smeltede alle disse drømme sammen i ubevidsthed og glemsel, som efter Napoleons læge Larreys mening langt snarere ville ende med døden end med helbredelse.
»Han er et nervøst, galdesygt subjekt,« sagde Larrey, »og vil ikke overleve.«
Og fyrst Andrej blev sammen med andre dødsmærkede overladt til beboerne i egnen.

english.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: On the Pratzen Heights, where he had fallen with the flagstaff in his hand, Prince Andrew Bolkonski lay bleeding heavily, unconsciously letting out a gentle, pitiful, childlike moan.
Toward evening he stopped moaning and became completely still. He had no idea how long he had been unconscious. Suddenly he felt alive again, aware of a burning, tearing pain in his head.

"Where is it, that vast sky I never knew until now, but saw today?" was his first thought. "And I never knew this suffering either," he thought. "Yes, I knew nothing, absolutely nothing until now. But where am I?"

He listened and heard the sound of horses approaching, along with voices speaking French. He opened his eyes. Above him was the same vast sky with clouds that had risen higher still, and between them shone an endless blue infinity. He did not turn his head and did not see those who, judging by the hoofbeats and voices, had ridden up and stopped near him.

It was Napoleon, accompanied by two aides-de-camp. Bonaparte, riding across the battlefield, had given final orders to strengthen the batteries firing at the Augesd Dam, and was now surveying the dead and wounded left on the field.
"Fine men!" Napoleon remarked, looking at a dead Russian grenadier who lay facedown with a blackened neck, one stiffened arm flung wide.
"The ammunition for the guns in position is exhausted, Your Majesty," said an adjutant who had come from the batteries firing at Augesd.

"Have some brought from the reserve," said Napoleon, and having walked on a few steps, he stopped before Prince Andrew, who lay on his back with the flagstaff dropped beside him. (The flag itself had already been taken by the French as a trophy.)
"That's a fine death!" said Napoleon, gazing at Bolkonski.

Prince Andrew understood that this was said about him and that it was Napoleon who said it. He heard the speaker addressed as Sire. But he heard the words the way one might hear the buzzing of a fly. Not only did they not interest him — he paid no attention to them at all and immediately forgot them. His head was burning, he felt himself bleeding to death, and he saw above him the distant, vast, everlasting sky. He knew it was Napoleon — his hero — but at that moment Napoleon seemed to him such a small, insignificant creature compared with what was happening now between himself and that vast infinite sky with its drifting clouds. At that moment it meant nothing to him who might be standing over him or what was said of him. He was only glad that people were near him, and he only wished they would help him and bring him back to life, which now seemed so beautiful, since today he had learned to see it so differently. He gathered all his strength, trying to stir and make a sound. He weakly moved his leg and let out a faint, sickly groan that aroused his own pity.
"Ah! He is alive," said Napoleon. "Lift this young man up and carry him to the dressing station."
Having said this, Napoleon rode on to meet Marshal Lannes, who, hat in hand, rode up smiling to the Emperor to congratulate him on the victory.

Prince Andrew remembered nothing more: he lost consciousness from the terrible pain of being lifted onto the stretcher, the jolting while being carried, and the probing of his wound at the dressing station. He did not regain consciousness until late in the day, when he was carried along with other wounded and captured Russian officers to the hospital. During this transfer he felt a little stronger and was able to look around and even speak.

The first words he heard on coming to his senses were from a French convoy officer, who said rapidly: "We must stop here: the Emperor will pass this way shortly, and it will please him to see these prisoners."
"There are so many prisoners today — nearly the whole Russian army — he's probably tired of them," said another officer.
"All the same! They say this one is the commander of all Emperor Alexander's Guards," said the first, pointing to a Russian officer in the white uniform of the Horse Guards.
Bolkonski recognized Prince Repnin, whom he had met in Petersburg society. Beside him stood a nineteen-year-old boy, also a wounded officer of the Horse Guards.
Bonaparte came galloping up and pulled his horse to a stop.
"Which is the senior?" he asked, seeing the prisoners.
They named the colonel, Prince Repnin.
"You are the commander of Emperor Alexander's Horse Guards regiment?" asked Napoleon.
"I commanded a squadron," replied Repnin.
"Your regiment fulfilled its duty honorably," said Napoleon.
"The praise of a great commander is a soldier's highest reward," said Repnin.
"I give it with pleasure," said Napoleon. "And who is that young man beside you?"
Prince Repnin named Lieutenant Sukhtelen.
After looking at him, Napoleon smiled.
"He's very young to come meddling with us."
"Youth is no obstacle to courage," Sukhtelen muttered in a failing voice.
"A splendid reply!" said Napoleon. "Young man, you will go far!"

Prince Andrew, who had also been brought forward before the Emperor's eyes to complete the display of prisoners, could not fail to attract his attention. Napoleon apparently remembered seeing him on the battlefield and, addressing him, again used the phrase "young man" that was connected in his memory with Prince Andrew.
"Well, and you, young man," he said. "How do you feel, mon brave?"

Though five minutes earlier Prince Andrew had been able to say a few words to the soldiers carrying him, now with his eyes fixed straight on Napoleon, he was silent. So insignificant at that moment seemed all the interests that consumed Napoleon, so petty did his hero himself appear with his trivial vanity and delight in victory, compared to the vast, fair, and kindly sky he had seen and understood, that he could not answer him.

Everything seemed so pointless and insignificant compared to the solemn chain of thoughts that weakness from blood loss, suffering, and the nearness of death stirred in him. Looking into Napoleon's eyes, Prince Andrew reflected on the insignificance of greatness, the unimportance of life which no one could understand, and the still greater unimportance of death, the meaning of which no living person could comprehend or explain.

The Emperor, without waiting for an answer, turned away and said to one of his officers as he left: "Have these gentlemen attended to and taken to my bivouac. Let my doctor, Larrey, examine their wounds. Farewell, Prince Repnin!" And he spurred his horse and galloped away.
His face glowed with self-satisfaction and pleasure.

The soldiers who had carried Prince Andrew had noticed the little gold icon Princess Mary had hung around her brother's neck, and they had taken it. But seeing how the Emperor favored the prisoners, they now hurried to return the holy image.
Prince Andrew did not see how or by whom it was put back, but the little icon with its thin gold chain suddenly appeared on his chest outside his uniform.

"It would be good," thought Prince Andrew, glancing at the icon his sister had hung around his neck with such feeling and devotion, "it would be good if everything were as clear and simple as it seems to Mary. How wonderful it would be to know where to seek help in this life, and what to expect after it, beyond the grave! How happy and at peace I would be if I could now say: 'Lord, have mercy on me!' But to whom should I say that? Either to a Power indefinable, incomprehensible, which I cannot even address, let alone put into words — the Great All or Nothing," he said to himself, "or to that God who has been sewn into this amulet by Mary! There is nothing certain, nothing at all — except the unimportance of everything I understand, and the greatness of something incomprehensible but supremely important."

The stretchers moved on. At every jolt he felt unbearable pain again; his fever rose and he became delirious. Visions of his father, his wife, his sister, and his future son, the tenderness he had felt the night before the battle, the figure of the insignificant little Napoleon, and above all the vast sky — these became the main subjects of his fevered imaginings.

The quiet domestic life and peaceful happiness of Bald Hills appeared before him. He was already enjoying that happiness when that little Napoleon had suddenly appeared with his unsympathetic expression of narrow-minded delight at others' misery, and doubts and torments had followed, and only the heavens promised peace. Toward morning all these dreams dissolved and merged into the chaos and darkness of unconsciousness and oblivion, which in the opinion of Napoleon's doctor, Larrey, was far more likely to end in death than in recovery.
"He is a nervous, bilious subject," said Larrey, "and will not recover."
And Prince Andrew, along with others who were fatally wounded, was left to the care of the local inhabitants.
